description: Representative pre-meal-planning dataset for the Agent Action Plan 0.9.1 dual-ledger equivalence and preservation gate. Every row is synthetic: the user ids are uid-shaped but belong to no Firebase project, the addresses are @example.com, and the one avatar is the base64 of the ASCII text 'fake-avatar-pixels'. The rows cover only tables that exist BEFORE the 20260908000000_meal_planning migration, and they deliberately carry none of that migration's additive columns (meal_entries.meal_plan_meal_id, catalog_food_id, recipe_version_id, nutrition_provenance) and none of its sixteen new tables, so the gate can load this dataset into a database that has only 20260706000000_init applied, migrate it by either ledger, and prove that every legacy row survives byte-for-byte and that no additive column was silently backfilled. Loaded only into the disposable databases the gate creates and drops; never into a development, shadow or production database.

type_notes.annotation_field: Every row may carry a 'note' field. It is documentation, not a column: the loader strips it and rejects any OTHER key that is not a real column of the target table, so a fixture that drifts from the schema fails loudly instead of silently dropping data.
type_notes.uuid_scheme: Uuid primary keys are deterministic and encode their table in the first group so foreign keys read at a glance: 00000001=foods, 00000002=meals, 00000003=meal_entries, 00000004=user_exercises, 00000005=templates, 00000006=workout_days, 00000007=daily_exercises, 00000008=exercise_sets, 00000009=personal_records, 0000000a=runs, 0000000b=run_splits, 0000000c=run_personal_records, 0000000d=body_weight_entries. The last group is a per-table counter.
type_notes.user_ids: users.id is TEXT (a Firebase uid in production), so the three fixture users are 28-character alphanumeric strings that are obviously synthetic.
type_notes.bigint_columns: workout_days.updated_at and runs.updated_at are BigInt. They are written here as JSON numbers of epoch milliseconds, all below 2^53 so no precision is lost by a JSON parser. A raw pg loader may pass them straight through (node-postgres sends parameters as text and PostgreSQL casts to int8); a Prisma-based loader must wrap them in BigInt(...).
type_notes.date_columns: Columns typed @db.Date (meals.date, meal_entries.date, workout_days.date, exercise_sets.completed_at) are bare 'YYYY-MM-DD' strings. Every other temporal column is a full ISO-8601 instant with an explicit Z.
type_notes.explicit_timestamps: Every created_at, updated_at, logged_at, fetched_at and achieved_at value is written explicitly even though the schema defaults them to now(). That is what makes the gate's cross-ledger row hashes comparable: a defaulted now() would differ between the two disposable databases and would fail the comparison for a reason that has nothing to do with the migration.
type_notes.macro_units: foods and meal_entries macros are integers (Int columns). meal_entries calories/protein_g/carbs_g/fat_g are PER SERVING; as-eaten values are round(perServing * servings), which is how src/services/nutrition.service.ts reads them.
type_notes.soft_deletes: deleted_at is @db.Timestamptz(6) on foods, meals, meal_entries and user_exercises. Rows with a non-null deleted_at are soft-deleted and must stay in the table through the migration.
type_notes.no_weight_unit: body_weight_entries has no unit column in this schema and none is invented here. The stored number is unit-less by design, which is exactly the ambiguity the plan's weigh-in prefill policy has to live with.

users.note: All four targets set, plus an avatar. The 'complete targets' profile: the only profile the planner may generate for, and the one whose targets Account, the Diary and the planner must all report identically.

Calories only, the three macro targets null. The 'partial targets' profile: a legacy account that set a calorie goal years ago, which must read back as partially set rather than as complete or as absent.
All four targets null. The 'no targets' profile: the user who never opted in, whose local fallback must keep working and whose columns must stay null after the migration.

foods.name: Greek yogurt, plain
foods.note: source 'manual'. Its name is duplicated by a different owner's food below, so any query that forgets its user_id predicate returns two rows instead of one.

foods.name: Sourdough toast
foods.note: source 'label_scan', and the one food whose updated_at differs from its created_at.

foods.name: Chobani Greek Yogurt, plain nonfat
foods.note: source 'branded', the only food carrying a brand. A branded row is client-supplied nutrition, so after the release it must still earn no source-backed provenance label.

foods.name: Greek yogurt, plain
foods.note: source 'seed', and the contested half of the duplicated name: same name and macros as user one's food, different owner and different id.

foods.name: Sheet-pan salmon
foods.note: Soft-deleted food that a LIVE diary entry still points at. Deleting a personal food must not erase the diary history that referenced it, so both this row and that entry's food_id have to survive the migration.

foods.name: Overnight oats
foods.note: Orphan food: owned by the no-targets user and referenced by no diary entry. It proves the migration touches foods that nothing joins to.

meals.name: Breakfast
meals.note: Start of the complete four-bucket day. sort_order follows DEFAULT_MEALS in src/services/nutrition.service.ts: Breakfast 0, Lunch 1, Dinner 2, Snack 3.

meals.name: Snack
meals.note: The Snack bucket exists on this day, which is what a planned snack needs in order to be logged into an existing meal.

meals.name: Breakfast
meals.note: Start of the deliberately Snack-LESS day: only Breakfast, Lunch and Dinner exist, so reading this day exercises the lazy backfill in nutrition.service.ts that creates the missing default bucket on demand.

meals.name: Breakfast
meals.note: The only bucket of the zero-calorie day. Its live entries sum to 0 kcal, so the history aggregate (which filters HAVING SUM(...) > 0) must skip 2026-02-12 entirely while the rows stay in the table.

meals.name: Pre-workout
meals.note: Soft-deleted CUSTOM meal (a name outside DEFAULT_MEALS, sort_order past the defaults) that still contains a live entry. Both rows must survive: the parent is deleted, the child is not, and no cascade or cleanup may run during the migration.

meals.name: Breakfast
meals.note: Second owner, same date and same bucket name as user one's meal above. Any day query missing its user_id predicate returns both users' meals.

user_exercises.name: Barbell Bench Press
user_exercises.note: Global exercise: user_id is NULL, which the schema allows and which makes this the one row in the whole fixture that belongs to no user. It is referenced by a user-owned daily_exercise and by user-owned records, so a migration that tightened this column would break both.

user_exercises.name: Rowing Machine
user_exercises.note: Soft-deleted exercise that a personal record still points at, so strength history survives hiding the exercise. The six logging_type values across this collection are the vocabulary src/services/exercise.service.ts accepts.

templates.name: Push Day
templates.note: exercise_ids is a plain String[] rather than a foreign key, so the array contents are data the migration must preserve verbatim. tagline is NOT NULL in this schema.

templates.name: Push Day
templates.note: Same template name as user one's. The unique key is (user_id, name), so this row only loads if ownership is part of the constraint.

workout_days.note: Synced day with a real epoch-millisecond BigInt updated_at.
Unsynced day at the column default 0, the value every pre-sync row carries.
Second owner on the same date as the first row: the unique key is (user_id, date). has_synced is explicitly NULL, which the nullable Boolean allows and which is distinct from false.

runs.note: Fully populated GPS run with splits and an encoded polyline. run_type stays 'OUTDOOR' and source is 'GPS' because those are the only values the shipped code produces; no third value is invented here.

runs.notes: Entered by hand after the watch failed, so there is no trace.
runs.note: The sparse counterpart: a hand-entered run with every optional metric null, no splits, and free-text notes. Together the two rows cover both source values and both ends of the nullability of this table.

body_weight_entries.note: logged_at is a full instant rather than a day key, so two weigh-ins can share a date. There is no unit column in this schema and none is added here.
Second weigh-in on the same date as the first: the latest weigh-in is the one a prefill would read, and picking it requires ordering by logged_at, not by date.
The no-targets user's only row in the whole fixture: an account that weighs in but has never logged food or set a target.

ai_usage.note: Composite primary key (user_id, day) with day as a 'YYYY-MM-DD' UTC string rather than a date column. Meal planning issues no request-time model calls, so this ledger must be untouched by the migration.
Same day as the first row for a different user, which is the half of the composite key that is easy to lose.

usda_api_cache.note: Raw vendor response cache keyed by request. payload is a JSON object (never a bare array: a raw pg loader would send a top-level array as a PostgreSQL array literal rather than as JSON). This table pre-dates the catalog tables and must not be migrated into them.

daily_exercises.note: 'order' is a reserved SQL word, so any loader or migration touching this table has to quote the identifier.
order is explicitly NULL, which the nullable column allows and which is not the same stored value as the default 0.

exercise_sets.note: Warm-up set. completed_at is @db.Date, a day key rather than an instant.
Working set with a fractional RPE; it is the set three of the personal records below were achieved on.
Bodyweight-reps set: no weight and no added weight, which is what distinguishes a max-reps record from a max-weight one.
Duration-only set with completed_at NULL: a set can be marked completed without ever being stamped with a day.
The second owner's set, carrying weight, duration and distance at once so every numeric column in this table is populated somewhere in the fixture.

meal_entries.name: Greek yogurt, plain
meal_entries.note: input_method 'library' with a fractional servings of 1.5, so as-eaten calories are round(100 * 1.5) = 150 and a migration that rounded the stored per-serving value instead would change the day total.

meal_entries.name: Chobani Greek Yogurt, plain nonfat
meal_entries.note: input_method 'search' against a branded food: client-supplied nutrition that must never read back as source-backed.

meal_entries.name: Chicken burrito bowl
meal_entries.raw_input: chicken burrito bowl with brown rice, black beans and avocado
meal_entries.note: input_method 'ai_text' with food_id NULL and the original prompt in raw_input. An AI-logged entry is an estimate, so after the release it must render an 'Estimated' caption from input_method alone, with no provenance column set.

meal_entries.name: Sheet-pan salmon
meal_entries.note: Live entry pointing at the SOFT-DELETED food. The food_id must still be there after the migration: the relation is SetNull, so anything that actually deleted the food would silently blank this column.

meal_entries.name: Trail mix
meal_entries.raw_input: photo of a handful of trail mix
meal_entries.note: input_method 'ai_photo' in the Snack bucket with a half serving, completing the four legacy input methods this fixture covers.

meal_entries.name: Sourdough toast
meal_entries.note: Soft-deleted entry inside an otherwise populated meal, with updated_at moved to the deletion instant. It must stay in the table and stay out of every total.

meal_entries.name: Greek yogurt, plain
meal_entries.note: On the Snack-less day, so this day has history and still needs its missing bucket backfilled when read.

meal_entries.name: Lentil soup
meal_entries.note: servings 0.33 is the stored two-decimal representation of a one-third fraction chip, which is what the shipped serving helpers produce; it must survive as 0.33 and not be normalised.

meal_entries.name: Black coffee
meal_entries.note: The live half of the zero-calorie day: a real entry worth 0 kcal. Its day must be readable but must NOT appear in history, whose aggregate keeps only days summing above zero.

meal_entries.name: Sourdough toast
meal_entries.note: The deleted half of the zero-calorie day. It carries calories, so a history query that forgot the deleted_at filter would wrongly surface 2026-02-12.

meal_entries.name: Banana
meal_entries.note: Live entry whose PARENT MEAL is soft-deleted: the orphaned-by-soft-delete case. Both rows must survive the migration unchanged.

meal_entries.name: Greek yogurt, plain
meal_entries.note: The second owner's entry: same name, same date and the same bucket name as user one's first entry, pointing at that owner's own food. It is the row a query missing its user_id predicate would leak.

personal_records.note: One of the three records the same working set produced. The unique key is (user_id, exercise_id, record_type), so all three coexist.
A derived, non-integer value (185 * (1 + 5/30)), which is why value is a Float and must not be rounded by the migration.
reps_at_record is NULL for a timed record.
Two edges at once: the exercise is soft-deleted and exercise_set_id is NULL (the originating set was deleted). Strength history outlives both, and the sixth and last record_type is covered here.
The second owner's MAX_WEIGHT: the same record_type as user one's first row, which only coexists because ownership is part of the unique key.

run_splits.note: Five splits under one run, unique by (run_id, split_number). The last split leaves pace_sec_per_km NULL so the nullable column is exercised.

run_personal_records.note: The one record type where a lower value is better, so a migration that re-derived records from runs could plausibly get its direction wrong.
The second owner's MAX_DISTANCE: same record_type as user one's, distinct because the unique key is (user_id, record_type).
run_id is NULL: the relation is SetNull, so a record can outlive the run that set it. All three run record types are covered across this collection.
